items.stem: What colour change is seen when water is added to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate?
items.answer: white to blue
items.markingKey: CuSO₄ + 5H₂O → CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue).

items.stem: What colour change is seen when hydrated cobalt(II) chloride is heated?
items.answer: pink to blue
items.markingKey: Water of crystallisation is removed: CoCl₂·6H₂O (pink) → CoCl₂ (blue).

items.stem: Explain why the test with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate shows that a liquid contains water but not that it is pure water.
items.answer: Any liquid containing water turns it blue; purity must be shown by a sharp boiling point of 100 °C (or melting point of 0 °C).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: detects water only; 1 mark: boiling point test for purity [2]

items.stem: Arjun heats a sample of hydrated cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl₂·xH₂O, to constant mass. Mass of crucible = 18.95 g; crucible + hydrated salt = 22.52 g; crucible + anhydrous salt = 20.90 g. Calculate the value of x. (Ar: Cl = 35.5, Co = 59, H = 1, O = 16)

Grace heats 2.50 g of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals, CuSO₄·5H₂O, in an evaporating basin until a white powder remains. Water is then added drop by drop to the cooled powder. (Ar: Cu = 64, H = 1, O = 16, S = 32) (a) Write the equation for the reversible reaction, including the ⇌ symbol. (b) State whether the forward reaction (heating) is endothermic or exothermic, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O (b) endothermic: heat must be supplied to remove the water

items.stem: What does the symbol ⇌ show in an equation?
items.answer: The reaction is reversible.
items.markingKey: ⇌ means the reaction can go in both directions.

items.stem: Explain why heating blue copper(II) sulfate crystals is described as a reversible reaction.
items.answer: Heating removes the water to give white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate; adding water to the white powder re-forms the blue hydrated salt.

items.stem: Explain why the dehydration of hydrated copper(II) sulfate is endothermic and its rehydration is exothermic.
items.answer: Energy is needed to break the bonds to the water of crystallisation; the same amount is released when the water re-bonds (the mixture gets hot).

items.stem: Aisha heats a sample of hydrated cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl₂·xH₂O, to constant mass. Mass of crucible = 17.08 g; crucible + hydrated salt = 20.65 g; crucible + anhydrous salt = 19.03 g. Calculate the value of x. (Ar: Cl = 35.5, Co = 59, H = 1, O = 16)

Leila heats a sample of hydrated zinc sulfate, ZnSO₄·xH₂O, to constant mass. Mass of crucible = 18.95 g; crucible + hydrated salt = 22.39 g; crucible + anhydrous salt = 20.88 g. Calculate the value of x. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16, S = 32, Zn = 65)

Samuel heats a sample of hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO₄·xH₂O, to constant mass. Mass of crucible = 18.95 g; crucible + hydrated salt = 21.90 g; crucible + anhydrous salt = 20.39 g. Calculate the value of x. (Ar: H = 1, Mg = 24, O = 16, S = 32)

Diego heats 2.50 g of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals, CuSO₄·5H₂O, in an evaporating basin until a white powder remains. Water is then added drop by drop to the cooled powder. (Ar: Cu = 64, H = 1, O = 16, S = 32) (a) Describe what is observed when the water is added. (b) State whether the forward reaction (heating) is endothermic or exothermic, giving a reason. (c) Calculate the mass of water lost.
items.answer: (a) white powder turns blue; the mixture gets warm (b) endothermic: heat must be supplied to remove the water (c) 0.900 g

items.stem: Mohammed heats 5.00 g of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals, CuSO₄·5H₂O, in an evaporating basin until a white powder remains. Water is then added drop by drop to the cooled powder. (Ar: Cu = 64, H = 1, O = 16, S = 32) (a) Write the equation for the reversible reaction, including the ⇌ symbol. (b) State whether the forward reaction (heating) is endothermic or exothermic, giving a reason. (c) Calculate the mass of water lost. (d) Suggest how cobalt(II) chloride could be used for the same purpose.
items.answer: (a) CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O (b) endothermic: heat must be supplied to remove the water (c) 1.80 g (d) blue anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride turns pink with water

items.stem: Which statement about a reaction at dynamic equilibrium is correct?
options: The forward and reverse reactions have stopped.
Only the forward reaction takes place.
The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.
The concentrations of reactants and products are always equal.
items.answer: The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.
items.markingKey: Dynamic equilibrium: both reactions continue at equal rates; concentrations stay constant.

items.stem: Explain why an equilibrium is described as dynamic.
items.answer: Both the forward and reverse reactions are still happening, at the same rate, so the concentrations do not change even though particles are constantly reacting.

items.stem: Explain why equilibrium cannot be reached in an open beaker if one of the products is a gas.
items.answer: The gas escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot take place; the system is not closed.

items.stem: The hydration of ethene is represented by C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g), ΔH = −45 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: increase temperature; add a catalyst; increase pressure.
items.answer: increase temperature: yield decreases; add a catalyst: yield does not change; increase pressure: yield increases
items.markingKey: increase temperature → decreases (the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature); add a catalyst → does not change (a catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally; equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged); increase pressure → increases (there are 2 mol of gas on the left and 1 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules). 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: The decomposition of phosphorus pentachloride is represented by PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), ΔH = +93 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: decrease pressure; increase pressure; increase temperature.
items.answer: decrease pressure: yield increases; increase pressure: yield decreases; increase temperature: yield increases
items.markingKey: decrease pressure → increases (there are 1 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards more gas molecules); increase pressure → decreases (there are 1 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules); increase temperature → increases (the forward reaction is endothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature). 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: The formation of hydrogen iodide is represented by H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), ΔH = −10 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: decrease temperature; increase temperature; add a catalyst; decrease pressure.
items.answer: decrease temperature: yield increases; increase temperature: yield decreases; add a catalyst: yield does not change; decrease pressure: yield does not change
items.markingKey: decrease temperature → increases (the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction); increase temperature → decreases (the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature); add a catalyst → does not change (a catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally; equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged); decrease pressure → does not change (there are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 and 2), so pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium). 1 mark each [4]

items.stem: Felix studies the Contact process: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −196 kJ/mol. The reaction is carried out in a closed system. (a) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the yield. (b) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the yield.
items.answer: (a) yield decreases: the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature (b) yield increases: there are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Isla studies the formation of hydrogen iodide: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), ΔH = −10 kJ/mol. The reaction is carried out in a closed system. (a) Explain what is meant by dynamic equilibrium. (b) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the yield. (c) Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate even if it lowers the yield.
items.answer: (a) forward and reverse rates equal; concentrations constant; both reactions continue (b) yield does not change: there are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 and 2), so pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium (c) particles faster: more frequent, more energetic collisions
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: What is needed for a reversible reaction to reach equilibrium?
items.answer: a closed system
items.markingKey: No substances can enter or leave.

items.stem: What is the effect of a catalyst on the position of equilibrium?
items.answer: There is no effect.
items.markingKey: It increases both rates equally.

items.stem: Explain why a catalyst is used in industry even though it does not change the yield at equilibrium.
items.answer: It increases the rate so equilibrium is reached faster, allowing a lower temperature to be used and saving time and energy.

items.stem: A student says that at equilibrium there are equal amounts of reactants and products. Explain the error.
items.answer: At equilibrium the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal; the amounts are constant but usually not equal.

items.stem: Consider the formation of hydrogen iodide: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), ΔH = −10 kJ/mol. Predict and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium and on the yield of HI when the concentration of H₂ is increased.
items.answer: Equilibrium shifts to the right; yield of HI increases. Reason: the equilibrium shifts to the right to oppose the change (use up the added reactant / replace the removed product).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: direction/yield; 1 mark: reason [2]

items.stem: Consider the hydration of ethene: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ C₂H₅OH(g), ΔH = −45 kJ/mol. Predict and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium and on the yield of C₂H₅OH when decrease temperature.
items.answer: Equilibrium shifts to the right; yield of C₂H₅OH increases. Reason: the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: direction; 1 mark: effect on yield; 1 mark: reason [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a catalyst is used in industry even though it does not change the yield at equilibrium. (b) Explain why an equilibrium is described as dynamic.
items.answer: (a) It increases the rate so equilibrium is reached faster, allowing a lower temperature to be used and saving time and energy. (b) Both the forward and reverse reactions are still happening, at the same rate, so the concentrations do not change even though particles are constantly reacting.

items.stem: Consider the water–gas shift reaction: CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g), ΔH = −41 kJ/mol. Predict and explain the effect on the position of equilibrium and on the yield of CO₂ and H₂ when CO₂ is removed as it forms.
items.answer: Equilibrium shifts to the right; yield of CO₂ and H₂ increases. Reason: the equilibrium shifts to the right to oppose the change (use up the added reactant / replace the removed product).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: direction; 1 mark: effect on yield; 1 mark: reason [3]

items.stem: The oxidation of nitrogen monoxide is represented by 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), ΔH = −114 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: decrease pressure; increase pressure; increase temperature.
items.answer: decrease pressure: yield decreases; increase pressure: yield increases; increase temperature: yield decreases
items.markingKey: decrease pressure → decreases (there are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards more gas molecules); increase pressure → increases (there are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules); increase temperature → decreases (the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature). 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: The Haber process is represented by N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: increase pressure; decrease pressure; decrease temperature.
items.answer: increase pressure: yield increases; decrease pressure: yield decreases; decrease temperature: yield increases
items.markingKey: increase pressure → increases (there are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules); decrease pressure → decreases (there are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards more gas molecules); decrease temperature → increases (the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction). 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: The Haber process is represented by N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: increase temperature; decrease pressure; decrease temperature.
items.answer: increase temperature: yield decreases; decrease pressure: yield decreases; decrease temperature: yield increases
items.markingKey: increase temperature → decreases (the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature); decrease pressure → decreases (there are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards more gas molecules); decrease temperature → increases (the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction). 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: A sealed syringe contains an equilibrium mixture: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), ΔH = −58 kJ/mol. NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless. Predict and explain the colour change when the plunger of the sealed syringe is pushed in quickly and held.
items.answer: The mixture becomes paler: equilibrium shifts to the right because higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: colour change; 1 mark: direction; 1 mark: reason [3]

items.stem: The oxidation of nitrogen monoxide is represented by 2NO(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), ΔH = −114 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: decrease pressure; decrease temperature; increase pressure.
items.answer: decrease pressure: yield decreases; decrease temperature: yield increases; increase pressure: yield increases
items.markingKey: decrease pressure → decreases (there are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards more gas molecules); decrease temperature → increases (the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction); increase pressure → increases (there are 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules). 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: A sealed syringe contains an equilibrium mixture: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g), ΔH = −58 kJ/mol. NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless. Predict and explain the colour change when the sealed syringe is placed in iced water.
items.answer: The mixture becomes paler: equilibrium shifts to the right because the exothermic direction is favoured at lower temperature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: colour change; 1 mark: direction; 1 mark: reason [3]

items.stem: Daniel studies steam reforming of methane: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔH = +206 kJ/mol. The reaction is carried out in a closed system. (a) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the yield. (b) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the pressure on the yield.
items.answer: (a) yield increases: the forward reaction is endothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature (b) yield decreases: there are 2 mol of gas on the left and 4 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2] (b) 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Noah studies steam reforming of methane: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔH = +206 kJ/mol. The reaction is carried out in a closed system. (a) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the yield. (b) Explain the effect of a catalyst on the rate and on the yield. (c) Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate even if it lowers the yield. (d) Suggest why the system must be closed.
items.answer: (a) yield increases: the forward reaction is endothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature (b) rate increases (equilibrium reached sooner); yield unchanged (c) particles faster: more frequent, more energetic collisions (d) so that no reactants or products escape, allowing equilibrium to be established
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2] (b) [2] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: What are the typical conditions used in the Haber process?
items.answer: 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst
items.markingKey: Compromise conditions for rate, yield and cost.

items.stem: Explain why a temperature of about 450 °C is used in the Haber process even though a lower temperature gives a higher yield.
items.answer: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would increase yield, but the rate would be too slow; 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower T higher yield (exothermic); 1 mark: rate too slow; 1 mark: compromise [3]

items.stem: Explain why a pressure of 200 atm is used in the Haber process rather than 1000 atm.
items.answer: Higher pressure increases yield (fewer gas molecules on the right) and rate, but very high pressures are expensive to produce and dangerous; 200 atm is a compromise.

items.stem: Sulfuric acid is made in Madrid by the Contact process. The key step is 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH = −196 kJ/mol. (a) State the sources of the sulfur dioxide and oxygen. (b) Explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the yield of SO₃.
items.answer: (a) burning sulfur (or roasting sulfide ores); air (b) decreases: forward reaction exothermic so equilibrium shifts left
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which temperature is used in the Haber process?
items.markingKey: Haber process: 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst; N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.

items.stem: Explain why the Contact process uses a low pressure of about 2 atm.
items.answer: The equilibrium yield of SO₃ is already very high (about 99%) at low pressure, so the extra cost of high pressure is not justified.

items.stem: Explain why unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled in the Haber process.
items.answer: Only about 15% conversion is achieved per pass; recycling the unreacted gases means they are eventually converted, saving raw materials and money.

items.stem: Explain how ammonia is separated from the unreacted gases in the Haber process.
items.answer: The mixture is cooled; ammonia condenses to a liquid (higher boiling point) while nitrogen and hydrogen remain as gases.

items.stem: Explain the choice of pressure used in the Contact process.
items.answer: 3 mol of gas form 2 mol, so higher pressure would favour SO₃, but the yield is already about 99% at 2 atm, so high pressure is not worth the cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: effect on yield with reason; 1 mark: effect on rate; 1 mark: compromise/cost [3]

items.stem: Which substance is used to test for the presence of water?
items.answer: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate

items.stem: Explain how cobalt(II) chloride paper can be used to show the humidity of the air.

items.stem: The decomposition of phosphorus pentachloride is represented by PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), ΔH = +93 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: add a catalyst; decrease pressure; increase pressure.
items.answer: add a catalyst: yield does not change; decrease pressure: yield increases; increase pressure: yield decreases
items.markingKey: add a catalyst → does not change (a catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally; equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged); decrease pressure → increases (there are 1 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards more gas molecules); increase pressure → decreases (there are 1 mol of gas on the left and 2 on the right; the equilibrium shifts towards fewer gas molecules). 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: The formation of nitrogen monoxide in car engines is represented by N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g), ΔH = +181 kJ/mol. For each change, predict the effect on the equilibrium yield of products: increase temperature; decrease temperature; decrease pressure.
items.answer: increase temperature: yield increases; decrease temperature: yield decreases; decrease pressure: yield does not change
items.markingKey: increase temperature → increases (the forward reaction is endothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature); decrease temperature → decreases (the forward reaction is endothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction); decrease pressure → does not change (there are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 and 2), so pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium). 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the Contact process uses a low pressure of about 2 atm. (b) Explain how ammonia is separated from the unreacted gases in the Haber process.
items.answer: (a) The equilibrium yield of SO₃ is already very high (about 99%) at low pressure, so the extra cost of high pressure is not justified. (b) The mixture is cooled; ammonia condenses to a liquid (higher boiling point) while nitrogen and hydrogen remain as gases.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a temperature of about 450 °C is used in the Haber process even though a lower temperature gives a higher yield. (b) Explain how ammonia is separated from the unreacted gases in the Haber process.
items.answer: (a) The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would increase yield, but the rate would be too slow; 450 °C is a compromise between rate and yield. (b) The mixture is cooled; ammonia condenses to a liquid (higher boiling point) while nitrogen and hydrogen remain as gases.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: lower T higher yield (exothermic); 1 mark: rate too slow; 1 mark: compromise [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a catalyst is used in industry even though it does not change the yield at equilibrium. (b) A student says that at equilibrium there are equal amounts of reactants and products. Explain the error.
items.answer: (a) It increases the rate so equilibrium is reached faster, allowing a lower temperature to be used and saving time and energy. (b) At equilibrium the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal; the amounts are constant but usually not equal.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student says that at equilibrium there are equal amounts of reactants and products. Explain the error. (b) Explain why an equilibrium is described as dynamic.
items.answer: (a) At equilibrium the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal; the amounts are constant but usually not equal. (b) Both the forward and reverse reactions are still happening, at the same rate, so the concentrations do not change even though particles are constantly reacting.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a pressure of 200 atm is used in the Haber process rather than 1000 atm. (b) Explain why the Contact process uses a low pressure of about 2 atm.
items.answer: (a) Higher pressure increases yield (fewer gas molecules on the right) and rate, but very high pressures are expensive to produce and dangerous; 200 atm is a compromise.
